dimensions.name: S3/boto3 contract & environment reconnaissance

evidence.note: Environment recon (ls/pwd/python version) then wrote auth.py SigV4 directly from recall; correct broad understanding of header vs query signing but no probing of botocore's canonical-request construction.
Installed boto3 and used round-trips to discover contract facts (XML namespace breaking ElementTree.find, header casing) reactively during debugging rather than capturing them upfront.
Discovered SigV4-vs-Basic-auth mismatch and anonymous GET/HEAD-via-policy semantics only after tests failed — contract learning was reactive, not systematic.
Enumerated and verified the full required data-testid surface in the console HTML against the spec — concrete contract extraction.

Listed 'verify SigV4 byte-perfect', UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, and clock-skew as planned checks but never captured signing fixtures or systematically enumerated the error-code/edge surface; plan not converted into a reference.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent extracted concrete spec contract points (ETag format, EntityTooSmall, error codes, full testid list, health endpoint) and correctly recalled SigV4 header signing before implementing auth — squarely anchor 5. It did surface several real contract subtleties (XML namespaces, header casing, auth/anonymous semantics), but these were discovered reactively via boto3 debugging rather than through the deliberate signing-fixture capture and full-surface enumeration that anchor 8 requires, and no systematic external-contract reference was ever built. This places it at the 5 anchor with only mild movement toward 6.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & verifiable milestones

evidence.note: Opening enumerates all ~dozen subsystems and states foundations-first intent, establishing a real decomposition rather than a flat 'do S3/console/admin' list.
Builds in dependency-aware order — config/database and SigV4 auth before s3_handlers, then admin/workers/console, then main wiring and static files — so foundations precede dependents.

Front-loads foundational risk: catches DB schema flaw, SigV4 body-caching, route-ordering, and session-storage/worker-model issues early, though some (routing order) surfaced reactively rather than being planned.

Concrete acceptance checks exist per feature (versioning round-trip, 30-client concurrency, multipart ETag/EntityTooSmall, e2e), but applied ad-hoc via 'run comprehensive test' rather than pre-declared per milestone.

Repeated numbered 'remaining issues' lists act as a rolling to-do — living and revised, but a checklist rather than a sized milestone hierarchy; items recur (worker import) indicating loose sequencing.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent enumerates all major subsystems up front and sequences them foundations-first (storage/DB and SigV4 before multipart/versioning; console shell before views), with foundational risk front-loaded — clearly above the level-5 anchor. Concrete acceptance checks do appear (versioning round-trip, composite-ETag/EntityTooSmall, 30-client concurrency), but they emerge reactively via ad-hoc 'comprehensive test' runs rather than as a pre-declared milestone hierarchy with per-milestone done-criteria, and the plan stays a rolling checklist with some late-discovered ordering rework. This places it at 6 — between the sensible-ordering 5 and the explicit-milestone-hierarchy 8.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification against boto3 & browser

evidence.note: Built boto3 test scripts for core S3 ops and a comprehensive script covering XML error format, cross-tenant, CopyObject, multipart, versioning, tagging, policies, presigned, admin, console, audit — went well beyond happy-path curls.

Testing surfaced the XML-namespace bug that silently broke versioning/tagging/multipart; agent debugged versioning directly and re-tested (step 46) confirming fix — a real test→fix→retest loop, not assumption of correctness.
Repeatedly ran targeted boto3 SigV4 tests for bucket policy/CORS/lifecycle PUT/GET/DELETE and NoSuch* codes; caught case-sensitivity and Basic-auth-vs-SigV4 issues.
Ran a 30-concurrent-client load test (matching the spec's concurrency gate) and reported it passing before finalizing.

Console verification was only a static grep for data-testid presence plus HTTP-level console API checks — no browser/DOM-driven side-effect testing, the key gap vs. the level-8 anchor and the actual browser grader.

Final e2e boto3+HTTP test covering ranged GET, conditional ops, ListObjectsV2 params, EntityTooSmall, versioning/delete markers — but as another one-off script rather than a consolidated repeatable suite; some earlier outputs were truncated/unobserved.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent ran the real boto3 client against core and many edge behaviors (ranged, EntityTooSmall, versioning/multipart ETag, cross-tenant/NoSuch* codes, presigned auth) plus a 30-client concurrency load test, using these checks to find and fix genuine bugs — clearly above the level-5 anchor. It stops short of level 8 because console verification was only a static testid grep with no DOM/browser-driven side-effect testing, and the checks were scattered one-off scripts (some with unobserved output) rather than a consolidated, repeatable milestone-gating harness. This places it at a 7, between the 5 and 8 anchors and leaning toward the strong correctness-side coverage.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across the horizon

evidence.note: Opens with an explicit enumeration of all required subsystems (S3 plane, admin, console, audit, lifecycle, policies, notifications, multi-tenancy, concurrency) and updates a running 'still need X' list as modules get created — a usable checklist of the horizon.
Recognizes versioning is stuck (PUT returns 200 but GET shows Suspended), stops retrying and debugs the root cause (XML namespace handling), i.e. names the impasse rather than looping blindly.

Maintains granular numbered 'remaining issues' lists that include specific contract items (multipart ETag format, EntityTooSmall, error XML/Content-Type, testids, presigned auth, 30-client concurrency) — fine-grained done-vs-remaining tracking.

Repeatedly re-discovers the SAME workers.py import bug (parse_xml_body, then httpx) across steps 65, 67, 76, 80 because earlier sed/fix scripts silently failed — a coverage-tracking lapse; no reliable check told it the fix had actually landed.

Declares 'Mark task complete' four separate times, each time reopening with 'critical remaining issues before marking complete' — the done picture oscillates, showing the completion criteria weren't stably tracked, though it did catch real gaps (worker duplication) each time.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent keeps a usable, and at times quite granular, checklist of subsystems and specific contract points (ETag rule, EntityTooSmall, testids, error codes), marks them off, and explicitly recognizes at least one genuine stuck state (versioning) by pausing to debug rather than retrying — behavior above the level-5 anchor. But its done-vs-remaining picture is not reliable: it thrashes on the same workers.py import bug across four steps and issues four premature 'complete' declarations it then has to reopen, indicating gaps in verifying that fixes landed and in knowing when the horizon was actually covered. That mix of solid checklist discipline undercut by import thrashing and unstable completion detection places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 6.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions

evidence.note: After first live start, diagnosed foundational bugs (SigV4 consuming request body, catch-all route shadowing console/admin) and rewrote auth body-caching and route ordering — design-level revision, not symptom patching.

Traced 'versioning shows Suspended' symptom to boto3's namespaced XML defeating ElementTree.find(); built parse_xml_body helper, propagated it across s3_handlers and workers, then re-verified versioning worked — anchor-8 style: verification failure treated as design signal, dependents re-checked.

Correctly attributed a failing test to the test using Basic auth instead of SigV4 (not the impl); separately recognized multi-worker + in-memory session store is architecturally broken and pivoted to DB-backed sessions.
Recognized --workers 4 would duplicate lifecycle/notification background workers and pivoted start.sh to single worker — a correctness-driven design decision.

Recurring workers.py import failure (parse_xml_body, httpx) handled by repeated ineffective sed/fix-script surface patches that kept silently failing; only at step 80 was the root cause (fix-script string mismatch) diagnosed. Same failure class recurred — anchor-3 flavor that caps the score below 8.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent repeatedly treats verification failures as signal about the underlying design and makes real pivots — body caching, route ordering, DB-backed sessions, single-worker, and especially the XML-namespace fix which it propagated across modules and then re-verified — placing it at the anchor-8 pattern for its foundational corrections. However, the persistent workers.py import bug was handled by a string of ineffective surface patches without verifying they landed (the same class of failure recurring across many steps), plus three premature completion declarations, showing the self-correction wasn't uniformly durable. This mix of strong design-level adaptation with a recurring surface-patch blind spot lands at 7, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Effort allocation across correctness gate & UX half

evidence.note: Console built in one short burst (console.py, index.html, app.js, styles.css) mid-way through; it is started but receives a tiny fraction of the ~80-step effort compared to the data plane.

Only substantive console revisit is a DB-backed session fix driven by an architectural concern, not a UX-quality investment; no work on visible side-effects, modals, or confirmation dialogs the rubric grades.
Console 'verification' is a grep confirming data-testid attributes exist — treated as a checkbox rather than exercising the testid-driven UX flows an automated browser checks.

Repeated 'remaining issues' punch-lists are almost entirely data-plane/correctness items (SigV4 byte-exactness, XML content-type, lifecycle timing, audit atomicity); console UX weight is never mentioned or re-prioritized.

Final verification and completion focus on boto3/admin/audit correctness; the console half is asserted done via 'all required data-testid attributes present' with no browser-side visible-side-effect testing.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent noticed both surfaces and got the console to a functional baseline (static files with all testids, console API tested), so it is above the level-3 floor. But allocation was driven by build momentum, not by the explicit half-score weight of the UX rubric: the console received a small slice of effort, was verified only by testid-presence and API calls rather than the browser-graded visible side-effects, and was never rebalanced toward as a first-class deliverable. That places it between the level-3 'allocates by default momentum, one surface under-resourced' and level-5 'consciously reserves time for both,' landing at 4.

rubric.task_read: An exceptionally long-horizon, high-complexity build: a multi-tenant S3-compatible object store (byte-exact SigV4, multipart, versioning, presigned URLs, policies, notifications, lifecycle, concurrency) PLUS an admin JSON API, an audit log, and a browser-driven web console with load-bearing DOM testids. Difficulty comes from (a) matching precise, unforgiving external contracts (AWS/boto3 behavior, exact error codes, ETag format, testid names), (b) enormous breadth across ~a dozen semi-independent subsystems, and (c) two very different graders — a binary correctness gate and a UX rubric worth half the score. A skilled practitioner would invest heavily in orientation, decomposition, and self-built verification, and sustain progress-tracking and course-correction across the whole horizon.

dimensions.name: S3/boto3 contract & environment reconnaissance
dimensions.description: Understanding the exact behaviors to match (SigV4 canonical request/signing, header vs query auth, ETag/error-code/XML semantics, testid contract, runtime harness) before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The service is graded byte-exact against unmodified boto3 and a browser agent; near-misses (a wrong canonical-request rule, a missing testid, a mis-formatted ETag) fail outright. Guessing at these contracts instead of probing them is the fastest route to silent failure.

anchors.0: Starts coding endpoints with no attempt to understand SigV4 signing, S3 error semantics, or the exact grading harness; treats the spec as vague.
anchors.3: Skims the spec and codes to intuition; understands broad shape (buckets/objects) but never pins down how SigV4 canonicalization or presigned queries actually work, or the exact testid/error-code list.
anchors.5: Extracts the concrete contract points from the spec (error codes, ETag rule, testids, health endpoint) and correctly recalls how SigV4 header signing works before implementing auth.
anchors.8: Actively probes the real contract — e.g. runs boto3/botocore to capture how it builds canonical requests, presigned queries, UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, and clock-skew; enumerates the full testid/error-code surface; understands versioning + delete-marker and multipart-ETag edge semantics before committing to a storage design.
anchors.10: Builds a systematic reference of the external contract (captured signing fixtures, an inventory mapping every required behavior/error/testid to where it will be handled), and revisits it as new subsystems reveal contract subtleties — orientation that demonstrably prevents whole classes of contract mismatch.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & verifiable milestones
dimensions.description: Breaking a ~dozen-subsystem build into an ordered hierarchy of sub-goals, each with an explicit done-check, and sequencing so foundations (auth, storage layout) precede dependents.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is far too large to hold as one push; without a dependency-aware plan (SigV4 and storage before multipart/versioning; console shell before views), an agent will build things in an order that forces rework or leaves whole areas unstarted at the horizon.

anchors.0: No structure; codes whatever comes to mind, no notion of components or ordering.
anchors.3: A flat, vague to-do ("do S3, do console, do admin") with no ordering rationale and no per-item done criteria.
anchors.5: Enumerates the major subsystems and tackles them in a sensible order (auth/storage first), with a rough sense of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy with dependency-aware sequencing and a concrete acceptance check per milestone (e.g. 'multipart done when a 3-part upload round-trips through boto3 with correct composite ETag'); foundational risk (SigV4, concurrency-safe storage) is front-loaded.
anchors.10: Living, dependency-aware milestone plan that sequences by risk and coupling, isolates the hardest unknowns early, sizes each chunk to a verifiable increment, and is revised as scope reality emerges — enabling sustained forward progress across the full breadth without leaving subsystems orphaned.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification against boto3 & browser
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks — boto3 round-trips, raw-HTTP error-code assertions, presign/multipart/versioning tests, concurrency load, console DOM/testid checks — rather than assuming endpoints work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Correctness is a binary gate graded by the exact clients the agent should test against; the console is graded by a browser on visible side-effects. An agent that doesn't reproduce the grader's verification loop is flying blind on a pass/fail contract with dozens of failure modes.

anchors.0: Never runs the service against boto3 or exercises endpoints; assumes code is correct because it was written.
anchors.3: Ad hoc manual curls or a couple of happy-path checks; no boto3 verification of signing, no error-code or edge-case checks, no console interaction test.
anchors.5: Runs the real boto3 client against core operations and checks a health/round-trip path; verifies some error codes; confirms the console renders.
anchors.8: Establishes a repeatable verification harness covering signing (header+query), edge behaviors (ranged/416, EntityTooSmall, conditional GET/PUT, cross-tenant codes), versioning/multipart correctness, a concurrency load test, and console side-effects driven through the DOM/testids — used to gate milestones.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, largely automated verification suite mirroring both graders (boto3 correctness + browser UX side-effects), including negative/error-path and concurrency/corruption checks, run continuously so regressions surface immediately; verification is designed to catch the hard-to-fake contract details, not just happy paths.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across the horizon
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture across all subsystems and required contract points, and detecting stuck/thrashing states (e.g. spinning on a SigV4 mismatch).
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a dozen subsystems and long execution, it is easy to lose track of which required behaviors/error codes/testids remain, or to burn the horizon re-debugging one signature mismatch. Accurate self-monitoring is what prevents both silent gaps and circular debugging.

anchors.0: No sense of overall progress; no tracking of what's left; repeats the same failing approach without noticing.
anchors.3: Vague mental sense of progress; frequently forgets whole required areas (notifications, lifecycle, an error code) or loops on a bug without recognizing it.
anchors.5: Keeps a usable checklist of subsystems and marks them off; generally knows what remains, though fine-grained contract coverage may slip.
anchors.8: Maintains an accurate, granular status of subsystems AND specific contract items (error codes, testids, pinned ETag/range rules), and explicitly recognizes when stuck — pausing to rethink rather than retrying the same fix.
anchors.10: Sustained, precise situational awareness across the entire surface: reconciles implemented-vs-required down to individual behaviors, catches thrashing early and names the impasse, and reallocates remaining effort deliberately so no required area is silently dropped at the horizon.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising design or approach when reality diverges — e.g. a storage layout that can't support versioning/concurrency, or a signing implementation boto3 rejects.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Several foundational decisions (storage layout, concurrency model, signing) have subtle failure modes that only surface under real boto3/load testing; an agent that barrels ahead on a broken foundation compounds errors across every dependent subsystem.

anchors.0: Ignores contradicting evidence (failing boto3 calls, corruption under load) and keeps building on the broken assumption.
anchors.3: Reacts only with surface patches to symptoms; never revisits the underlying design even when the same class of failure recurs.
anchors.5: When a check fails, diagnoses and fixes the actual cause, including occasionally revising a local design choice.
anchors.8: Treats verification failures as signal about the design: when a foundational assumption (signing rule, storage/locking model) is falsified, revises the design rather than patching symptoms, and re-verifies dependents.
anchors.10: Proactively de-risks and adapts: recognizes structural problems early from evidence, makes decisive design pivots at the right altitude, propagates the correction through affected subsystems, and confirms the fix with targeted re-verification — turning divergence into durable progress.

dimensions.name: Effort allocation across correctness gate & UX half
dimensions.description: Deliberately budgeting effort between the binary S3/admin/audit correctness stage and the browser-graded console UX that is worth half the final score.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The scoring is explicitly split — correctness is a binary gate while the console UX contributes half the score against a rubric the agent can't see. Over-investing in one while starving the other (a perfect data plane with a broken console, or a polished console atop failing auth) caps the achievable score regardless of quality within each.

anchors.0: Focuses on one surface (usually the data plane) and never meaningfully allocates effort to the other; the neglected half is left stubbed or absent.
anchors.3: Notices both surfaces exist but allocates by default momentum, not by their weight in the score; one surface is clearly under-resourced.
anchors.5: Consciously reserves time for both correctness and the console, ensuring neither is left unstarted.
anchors.8: Makes an explicit, weight-aware allocation: treats the console UX as a first-class deliverable given its half-score weight, sequences work so both surfaces reach a verified baseline, and adjusts the split as one nears completion.
anchors.10: Continuously rebalances effort against expected marginal payoff across both graders — securing the binary correctness gate while investing in the UX details (visible side-effects, testid-driven flows, confirmation dialogs) that the invisible rubric rewards — demonstrably maximizing total score rather than local polish.
